history: A budget was once a little leather bag. Old French bouge was a leather bag or purse, and bougette, a small one, is attested from the 12th century. English borrowed bougette as budget, ‘leather bag’, by the middle of the 15th century. Then the word went into politics: English used it for the annual statement of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and in 1733 a pamphlet was called The Budget opened. French borrowed the word back from English. In 1764 it was still used about English public finances, and only later about French ones. Today it is everyday French: le budget de l'État, le budget familial, and boucler son budget, ‘to make ends meet’.
historyEinfach: Budget comes from old French bougette, a small leather bag for money. English took the word, and later used it for the money plan of the government. Then French took the word back from English. Today you have a budget for the month: le budget familial.

elsewhere.text: Another round trip through English: a French bag went to London and came back as public finance.
